title: 1 Kings 14:1–20
context: When Jeroboam's son Abijah falls ill, Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh, the prophet who had first promised him the kingdom. Though Ahijah is blind, the LORD tells him who is coming. He delivers a heavy word: because Jeroboam has done evil above all before him, God will cut off his house, and Israel itself will one day be uprooted. The child will die as she enters the city, and he alone of Jeroboam's family will be mourned and buried, because in him there was "some good thing toward the LORD." The section closes with Jeroboam's death after twenty-two years.

verses.text: At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam became sick.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah, Jeroboam's son, falls sick. Arminian readers see a grieving father facing a crisis, a moment in which he could turn to God in repentance rather than only seek information.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the sickness becomes the occasion for God's word to confront Jeroboam again. God's providence brings the king face to face with his sin through personal sorrow.

verses.text: Jeroboam said to his wife, “Please get up and disguise yourself, so that you won’t be recognized as Jeroboam’s wife. Go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said that I would be king over this people.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam tells his wife to disguise herself and go to Ahijah, "who said that I would be king." Arminian readers see Jeroboam trusting the prophet's power while still avoiding open repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony: Jeroboam seeks the true prophet of the LORD while maintaining false worship. He wants God's word without submitting to God's rule.

verses.text: Take with you ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what will become of the child.”
verses.arminianNotes: She is to bring bread, cakes, and honey, the gifts of an ordinary visitor. Arminian readers note that the modest gift fits the disguise, part of a plan to obtain a favorable word without revealing who is asking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeroboam hopes to learn the child's future while concealing his identity. The attempt assumes God can be approached on human terms, an assumption the next verses overturn.

verses.text: Jeroboam’s wife did so, and arose and went to Shiloh, and came to Ahijah’s house. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were set by reason of his age.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahijah cannot see because of his age. Arminian readers note the human weakness of the prophet, which makes the disguise seem likely to work and highlights the role God will play.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the blind prophet will see more clearly than the disguised queen expects. God's knowledge does not depend on human eyesight.

verses.text: The LORD said to Ahijah, “Behold, Jeroboam’s wife is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Tell her such and such; for it will be, when she comes in, that she will pretend to be another woman.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ahijah who is coming and what to say. Arminian readers see God's knowledge of human plans and his readiness to speak truth to those who try to hide from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God knows every disguise and directs his prophet's words. No human scheme can conceal anything from God or bend his word to its purpose.

verses.text: So when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet as she came in at the door, he said, “Come in, Jeroboam’s wife! Why do you pretend to be another? For I am sent to you with heavy news.
verses.arminianNotes: "Come in, Jeroboam's wife! Why do you pretend to be another?" Arminian readers note the futility of trying to deceive God, and the compassion in Ahijah's warning that he brings "heavy news."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God exposes the disguise at once. The prophet's words remind readers that God sees through every attempt to manipulate him.

verses.text: Go, tell Jeroboam, ‘The LORD, the God of Israel, says: “Because I exalted you from among the people, and made you prince over my people Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: "Because I exalted you from among the people." Arminian readers note that God reminds Jeroboam of his gracious gift, the kingdom given to him, which deepened his responsibility to obey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's word begins with his own initiative: he raised Jeroboam up. The judgment that follows is measured against the grace Jeroboam received.

verses.text: and tore the kingdom away from David’s house, and gave it to you; and yet you have not been as my servant David, who kept my commandments, and who followed me with all his heart, to do that only which was right in my eyes,
verses.arminianNotes: God contrasts Jeroboam with David, "who kept my commandments." Arminian readers note that the promise in 11:38 was conditional, and that Jeroboam's failure to walk like David explains the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David is the standard not because he was sinless but because his heart followed God. Jeroboam's rejection of that pattern shows a heart turned away from God.

verses.text: but have done evil above all who were before you, and have gone and made for yourself other gods, molten images, to provoke me to anger, and have cast me behind your back,
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam has "done evil above all who were before you" and "cast me behind your back." Arminian readers see a deliberate rejection of God, the opposite of the wholehearted following God desired.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language of "other gods" and "molten images" describes the calves of 12:28. Jeroboam's sin is idolatry that leads a whole nation away from God.

verses.text: therefore, behold, I will bring evil on the house of Jeroboam, and will cut off from Jeroboam everyone who urinates on a wall, he who is shut up and he who is left at large in Israel, and will utterly sweep away the house of Jeroboam, as a man sweeps away dung until it is all gone.
verses.arminianNotes: God will cut off every male of Jeroboam's house and sweep it away. Arminian readers take this judgment formula as the text's own forceful language for complete dynastic ruin, fulfilled in 15:29.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the harsh imagery is a standard prophetic formula for a royal house's total end. The text stresses the seriousness of leading God's people into idolatry.

verses.text: The dogs will eat whoever belongs to Jeroboam who dies in the city; and the birds of the sky will eat whoever dies in the field, for the LORD has spoken it.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Those who die will be eaten by dogs and birds. Arminian readers note that being left unburied was a mark of disgrace in the ancient world, and the formula expresses dishonor and divine judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same formula recurs for later dynasties. Its point is the shame of a house that God has rejected, "for the LORD has spoken it," grounding the word in God's authority.

verses.text: Arise therefore, and go to your house. When your feet enter into the city, the child will die.
verses.arminianNotes: "When your feet enter into the city, the child will die." Arminian readers note the grief of this word and treat it pastorally; the child's death is not presented as his own punishment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the sorrow of the announcement. The next verse makes clear that the child's death comes with God's distinct mercy toward him, not condemnation of him.

verses.text: All Israel will mourn for him and bury him; for he only of Jeroboam will come to the grave, because in him there is found some good thing toward the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.
verses.arminianNotes: He alone will be buried and mourned, "because in him there is found some good thing toward the LORD." Arminian readers see God's gracious recognition of the child's goodness, sparing him the shame coming on his family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some interpreters connect Isaiah 57:1, "the righteous is taken away from the evil." They see God's mercy in the child's honorable burial; the text does not specify more, and both traditions avoid speculation beyond it.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD will raise up a king for himself over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam. This is the day! What? Even now.
verses.arminianNotes: God will raise up a king who will cut off Jeroboam's house. Arminian readers note that the warning comes with urgency ("Even now"), signaling that judgment is near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Baasha later fulfills this word (15:29). God raises up and removes kings according to his purposes, using even violent human actors to carry out his justice.

verses.text: For the LORD will strike Israel, as a reed is shaken in the water; and he will root up Israel out of this good land which he gave to their fathers, and will scatter them beyond the River, because they have made their Asherah poles, provoking the LORD to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: God will uproot Israel and scatter them "beyond the River" for their Asherah poles. Arminian readers see the nation's future exile as the consequence of persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the fulfillment in 2 Kings 17:23, when Israel "was carried away out of their own land to Assyria." The prophecy reaches far beyond Jeroboam's lifetime.

verses.text: He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he has sinned, and with which he has made Israel to sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: God will give Israel up "because of the sins of Jeroboam" with which he made Israel sin. Arminian readers note the weight of leadership: one king's choices shape a nation, yet the people share responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase becomes a refrain through Kings (compare 2 Kings 17:21–22). Jeroboam's sin is the pattern the northern kingdom never abandons.

verses.text: Jeroboam’s wife arose and departed, and came to Tirzah. As she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.
verses.arminianNotes: As she reaches the threshold at Tirzah, the child dies. Arminian readers note the painful fulfillment and the sorrow of a mother bearing the news home, calling for compassion rather than speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's word comes to pass at the exact moment spoken. The precision underlines the reliability of God's word, even when it brings grief.

verses.text: All Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the LORD’s word, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel buries and mourns him, as the LORD said. Arminian readers see God's honor given to the one child in Jeroboam's house who showed goodness toward him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the honorable burial fulfills Ahijah's word. God's distinction between this child and the rest of the house shows his justice and his mercy together.

verses.text: The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Jeroboam's acts are written in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note that the writer selects what serves his purpose, focusing on Jeroboam's relationship to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator points readers to other records for military and political details. Scripture's interest is in how kings stood before God, not in their worldly achievements.

verses.text: The days which Jeroboam reigned were twenty two years; then he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam reigns twenty-two years and dies, and Nadab succeeds him. Arminian readers note that the judgment on his house has not yet fallen, showing God's patience even toward a persistent sinner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nadab's reign will be short and end in the fulfillment of Ahijah's word (15:29). God's timing is his own, and his word does not fail.
